entries.29baa3df774749cbd341d23669f96661329d6ff5: <div sID="gen7867" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="22" osisID="1Chr.22" sID="1Chr.22"/> <div eID="gen7867" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7868" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen7869" type="x-p"/> "Out of the eater comes forth meat." It was upon occasion of the terrible judgment inflicted on Israel for the sin of David that God gave intimation of the setting up of another altar, and of the place where he would have the temple to be built, upon which David was excited with great vigour to make preparation for that great work, wherein, though he had long since designed it, it should seem, he had, of late, grown remiss, till awakened by the alarm of that judgment. The tokens of God's favour he received after those of his displeasure, I. Directed him to the place, <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.1">ver. 1</reference>. II. Encouraged and quickened him to the work. 1. He set himself to prepare for the building, <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.2-1Chr.22.5">ver. 2-5</reference>. 2. He instructed Solomon, and gave him a charge concerning this work, <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.6-1Chr.22.16">ver. 6-16</reference>. 3. He commanded the princes to assist him in it, <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.17-1Chr.22.19">ver. 17-19</reference>. There is a great deal of difference between the frame of David's spirit in the beginning of the former chapter and in the beginning of this. There, in the pride of his heart, he was numbering the people; here, in his humility, preparing for the service of God. There corruption was uppermost (but the well of living water in the soul, though it may be muddied, will work itself clear again); grace here has recovered the upper hand.
entries.3fe92198331880807be349696bbedf95477dc831: <div eID="gen7869" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen7868" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Preparations for the Temple. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1017.)</title> <div sID="gen7870" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Then David said, This <hi type="italic">is</hi> the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God, and this <hi type="italic">is</hi> the altar of the burnt offering for Israel. <hi type="super">2</hi> And David commanded to gather together the strangers that <hi type="italic">were</hi> in the land of Israel; and he set masons to hew wrought stones to build the house of God. <hi type="super">3</hi> And David prepared iron in abundance for the nails for the doors of the gates, and for the joinings; and brass in abundance without weight; <hi type="super">4</hi> Also cedar trees in abundance: for the Zidonians and they of Tyre brought much cedar wood to David. <hi type="super">5</hi> And David said, Solomon my son <hi type="italic">is</hi> young and tender, and the house <hi type="italic">that is</hi> to be builded for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">must be</hi> exceeding magnifical, of fame and of glory throughout all countries: I will <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> now make preparation for it. So David prepared abundantly before his death. <div eID="gen7870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7871" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The place fixed for the building of the temple (<reference osisRef="1Chr.22.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">Then David said,</hi> by inspiration of God, and as a declaration of his mind, <hi type="italic">This is the house of the Lord God.</hi> If a temple must be built for God, it is fit that it be left to him to choose the ground, for all the earth is his; and this is the ground he makes choice of-ground that pertained to a Jebusite, and perhaps there was not a spot of ground besides, in or about Jerusalem, that did so—a happy presage of the setting up of the gospel temple among the Gentiles. See <reference osisRef="Acts.15.16-Acts.15.17">Acts xv. 16, 17</reference>. The ground was a threshing-floor; for the church of the living God is his floor, his threshing, and <hi type="italic">the corn of his floor,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.21.10">Isa. xxi. 10</reference>. Christ's fan is in his hand, thoroughly to purge his floor. This is to be the house because this is the altar. The temple was built for the sake of the altar. There were altars long before there were temples. <div eID="gen7871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7872" type="x-p"/> II. Preparation made for that building. David must not build it, but he would do all he could towards it: He <hi type="italic">prepared abundantly before his death,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.5">v. 5</reference>. This intimates that the consideration of his age and growing infirmities, which showed him his death approaching, quickened him, towards his latter end, to be very diligent in making this preparation. What our hands find to do for God, and our souls, and our generation, let us do it with all our might before our death, because, after death, there is no device nor working. Now we are here told, <div eID="gen7872" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7873" type="x-p"/> 1. What induced him to make such preparation. Two things he considered:—(1.) That Solomon was young and tender, and not likely to apply with any great vigour to this business at first; so that, unless he found the wheels set a-going, he would be in danger of losing a great deal of time at first, the rather because, being young, he would be tempted to put it off; whereas, if he found the materials got ready to his hand, the most difficult part of the work would be over, and this would excite and encourage him to go about it in the beginnings of his reign. Note, Those that are aged and experienced should consider those that are young and tender, and provide them what help they can, that they may make the work of God as easy to them as possible. (2.) That the house must be exceedingly magnificent, very stately and sumptuous, strong and beautiful, every thing about it the best in its kind, and for a good reason, since it was intended for the honour of the great God, the Lord of the whole earth, and was to be a type of Christ, in whom all fulness dwells and in whom are hid all treasures. Men were then to be taught by sensible methods. The grandeur of the house would help to affect the worshippers with a holy awe and reverence of God, and would invite strangers to come to see it, and the wonder of the world, who thereby would be brought acquainted with the true God. Therefore it is here designed to be of fame and glory throughout all countries. David foretold this good effect of its being magnificent, <reference osisRef="Ps.68.29">Ps. lxviii. 29</reference> <hi type="italic">Because of thy temple at Jerusalem shall kings bring presents unto thee.</hi> <div eID="gen7873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7874" type="x-p"/> 2. What preparation he made. In general, he prepared abundantly, as we shall find afterwards; cedar and stones, iron and brass, are here specified, <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.2-1Chr.22.4">v. 2-4</reference>. Cedar he had from the Tyrians and the Zidonians. <hi type="italic">The daughter of Tyre shall be there with a gift,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.45.12">Ps. xlv. 12</reference>. He also got workmen together, <hi type="italic">the strangers that were in the land of Israel.</hi> Some think that he employed them because they were generally better artists, and more ingenious in manual operations, than the Israelites; or, rather, because he would not employ the free-born Israelites in any thing that looked mean and servile. They were delivered from the bondage of making bricks in Egypt, and must not return to hew stone. These strangers were proselytes to the Jewish religion, but, though not enslaved, they were not of equal dignity with Israelites.
entries.353442b297cb15212d76076568e67dd2061f581c: <div eID="gen7874" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Charge to Solomon. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1015.)</title> <div sID="gen7875" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Then he called for Solomon his son, and charged him to build a house for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel. <hi type="super">7</hi> And David said to Solomon, My son, as for me, it was in my mind to build a house unto the name of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> my God: <hi type="super">8</hi> But the word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> came to me, saying, Thou hast shed blood abundantly, and hast made great wars: thou shalt not build a house unto my name, because thou hast shed much blood upon the earth in my sight. <hi type="super">9</hi> Behold, a son shall be born to thee, who shall be a man of rest; and I will give him rest from all his enemies round about: for his name shall be Solomon, and I will give peace and quietness unto Israel in his days. <hi type="super">10</hi> He shall build a house for my name; and he shall be my son, and I <hi type="italic">will be</hi> his father; and I will establish the throne of his kingdom over Israel for ever. <hi type="super">11</hi> Now, my son, the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> be with thee; and prosper thou, and build the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God, as he hath said of thee. <hi type="super">12</hi> Only the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> give thee wisdom and understanding, and give thee charge concerning Israel, that thou mayest keep the law of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> thy God. <hi type="super">13</hi> Then shalt thou prosper, if thou takest heed to fulfil the statutes and judgments which the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> charged Moses with concerning Israel: be strong, and of good courage; dread not, nor be dismayed. <hi type="super">14</hi> Now, behold, in my trouble I have prepared for the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> a hundred thousand talents of gold, and a thousand thousand talents of silver; and of brass and iron without weight; for it is in abundance: timber also and stone have I prepared; and thou mayest add thereto. <hi type="super">15</hi> Moreover <hi type="italic">there are</hi> workmen with thee in abundance, hewers and workers of stone and timber, and all manner of cunning men for every manner of work. <hi type="super">16</hi> Of the gold, the silver, and the brass, and the iron, <hi type="italic">there is</hi> no number. Arise <hi type="italic">therefore,</hi> and be doing, and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> be with thee. <div eID="gen7875" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7876" type="x-p"/> Though Solomon was young and tender, he was capable of receiving instructions, which his father accordingly gave him, concerning the work for which he was designed. When David came to the throne he had many things to do, for the foundations were all out of course; but Solomon had only one thing in charge, and that was <hi type="italic">to build a house for the Lord God of Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.6">v. 6</reference>. Now, <div eID="gen7876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7877" type="x-p"/> I. David tells him why he did not do it himself. It was in his mind to do it (<reference osisRef="1Chr.22.7">v. 7</reference>), but God forbade him, because <hi type="italic">he had shed much blood,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.8">v. 8</reference>. Some think this refers to the blood of Uriah, which fastened such a reproach upon him as rendered him unworthy the honour of building the temple: but that honour was forbidden him before he had shed that blood; therefore it must be meant, as it is here explained, of the blood he shed in his wars (for he had been a man of war from his youth), which, though shed very justly and honourably in the service of God and Israel, yet made him unfit to be employed in this service, or rather less fit than another that had never been called to such bloody work. God, by assigning this as the reason of laying David aside from this work, showed how precious human life is to him, and intended a type of him who should build the gospel temple, not by <hi type="italic">destroying men's lives,</hi> but <hi type="italic">by saving them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.9.56">Luke ix. 56</reference>. <div eID="gen7877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7878" type="x-p"/> II. He gives him the reason why he imposed this task upon him. 1. Because God had designed him for it, nominated him as the man that should do it: <hi type="italic">A son shall be born to thee,</hi> that shall be called <hi type="italic">Solomon,</hi> and <hi type="italic">he shall build a house for my name,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.9-1Chr.22.10">v. 9, 10</reference>. Nothing is more powerful to engage us to any service for God, and encourage us in it, than to know that hereunto we are appointed. 2. Because he would have leisure and opportunity to do it. He should be a man of rest, and therefore should not have his time, or thoughts, or wealth, diverted from this business. He should have rest from his enemies abroad (none of them should invade or threaten him, or give him provocation), and he should have peace and quietness at home; and therefore let him build the house. Note, Where God gives rest he expects work. 3. Because God had promised to establish his kingdom. Let this encourage him to honour God, that God had honour in store for him; let him build up God's house, and God will build up his throne. Note, God's gracious promises should quicken and invigorate our religious service. <div eID="gen7878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7879" type="x-p"/> III. He delivers him an account of the vast preparations he had made for this building (<reference osisRef="1Chr.22.14">v. 14</reference>), not in a way of pride and vain glory (he speaks of it as a poor thing—<hi type="italic">I have, in my poverty, prepared,</hi> margin), but as an encouragement to Solomon to engage cheerfully in the work, for which so solid a foundation was laid. The treasure here mentioned of the 100,000 talents of gold, and 1,000 000 talents of silver, amounts to such an incredible sum that most interpreters either allow an error in the copy or think the talent here signifies no more than a plate or piece: <hi type="italic">ingots</hi> we call them. I am inclined to suppose that a certain number is here put for an uncertain, because it is said (<reference osisRef="1Chr.22.16">v. 16</reference>) that of the gold and silver, as well as of the brass and iron, there was no number, and that David here includes all the dedicated things (<reference osisRef="1Chr.18.11">ch. xviii. 11</reference>) which he designed <hi type="italic">for the house of the Lord,</hi> that is, not only for the building of it, but for the treasure of it; and putting all together, it might come pretty near what is here spoken of. Hundreds and thousands are numbers which we often use to express that which is very much, when yet we would not be understood strictly. <div eID="gen7879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7880" type="x-p"/> IV. He charges them to keep God's commandments and to take heed to his duty in every thing, <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.13">v. 13</reference>. He must not think by building the temple to purchase a dispensation to sin; no, on the contrary, his doing that would not be accepted, nor accounted of, if he did not <hi type="italic">take heed to fulfil the statutes which the Lord charged Moses with,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.13">v. 13</reference>. Though he was to be king of Israel, he must always remember that he was a subject to the God of Israel. <div eID="gen7880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7881" type="x-p"/> V. He encourages him to go about this great work, and to go on in it (<reference osisRef="1Chr.22.13">v. 13</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Be strong, and of good courage,</hi> Though it is a vast undertaking, thou needest not fear coming under the reproach of the foolish builder, who began to build and was not able to finish it; it is God's work, and it shall come to perfection. <hi type="italic">Dread not, nor be dismayed.</hi>" In our spiritual work, as well as in our spiritual warfare, we have need of courage and resolution. <div eID="gen7881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7882" type="x-p"/> VI. He quickens him not to rest in the preparations he had made, but to add thereto, <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.14">v. 14</reference>. Those that enter into the labours of others, and build upon their advantages, must still be improving. <div eID="gen7882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7883" type="x-p"/> VII. He prays for him: <hi type="italic">The Lord give thee wisdom and understanding, and give thee charge concerning Israel,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.12">v. 12</reference>. Whatever charge we have, if we see God giving us the charge and calling us to it, we may hope he will give us wisdom for the discharge of it. Perhaps Solomon had an eye to this prayer of his father for him, in the prayer he offered for himself: Lord, <hi type="italic">give me a wise and understanding heart.</hi> He concludes (<reference osisRef="1Chr.22.16">v. 16</reference>), <hi type="italic">Up, and be doing, and the Lord be with thee.</hi> Hope of God's presence must not slacken our endeavours. Though the Lord be with us, we must <hi type="italic">rise and be doing,</hi> and, if we do this, we have reason to believe he is and will be with us. Work out your salvation, and God will work in you.
entries.e1c7833e6ffc59304f467bb37bd8a7fae3d098e5: <div eID="gen7883" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Charge to the Princes of Israel. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1015.)</title> <div sID="gen7884" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> David also commanded all the princes of Israel to help Solomon his son, <hi type="italic">saying,</hi> <hi type="super">18</hi> <hi type="italic">Is</hi> not the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God with you? and hath he <hi type="italic">not</hi> given you rest on every side? for he hath given the inhabitants of the land into mine hand; and the land is subdued before the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and before his people. <hi type="super">19</hi> Now set your heart and your soul to seek the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> your God; arise therefore, and build ye the sanctuary of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God, to bring the ark of the covenant of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and the holy vessels of God, into the house that is to be built to the name of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <div eID="gen7884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7885" type="x-p"/> David here engages the princes of Israel to assist Solomon in the great work he had to do, and every one to lend him a hand towards the carrying of it on. Those that are in the throne cannot do the good they would, unless those about the throne set in with them. David would therefore have the princes to advise Solomon and quicken him, and make the work as easy to him as they could, by promoting it every one in his place. 1. He shows them what obligations they lay under to be zealous in this matter, in gratitude to God for the great things he had done for them. He had given them victory, and rest, and a good land for an inheritance, <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.18">v. 18</reference>. The more God has done for us the more we should study to do for him. 2. He presses that upon them which should make them zealous in it (<reference osisRef="1Chr.22.19">v. 19</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Set your heart and soul to seek God,</hi> place your happiness in his favour, and keep your eye upon his glory. Seek him as your chief good and highest end, and this <hi type="italic">with your heart and soul.</hi> Make religion your choice and business; and then you will grudge no pains nor cost to promote the building of his sanctuary." Let but the heart be sincerely engaged for God, and the head and hand, the estate and interest, and all will be cheerfully employed for him.  <chapter eID="1Chr.22"/> <div eID="gen7885" type="x-p"/>

entries.0d7b7e1177f43ef6bc7f555169aa90a7f5b80eb4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3839"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 22</title> <div sID="gen5510" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.1-1Chr.22.5">1Ch 22:1-5</reference>. David Prepares for Building the Temple.<div eID="gen5510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5511" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3839"/><hi type="bold">1. David said, This is the home of the Lord God--</hi>By the miraculous sign of fire from heaven, and perhaps other intimations, David understood it to be the will of God that the national place of worship should be fixed there, and he forthwith proceeded to make preparations for the erection of the temple on that spot. <div eID="gen5511" type="x-p"/>
entries.305a94c5a64f936dfda36909d141da3d0d90f637: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3840"/><div sID="gen5512" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3840"/><hi type="bold">2. David commanded to gather together the strangers--</hi>partly the descendants of the old Canaanites (<reference osisRef="2Chr.8.7-2Chr.8.10">2Ch 8:7-10</reference>), from whom was exacted a tribute of bond service, and partly war captives (<reference osisRef="2Chr.2.7">2Ch 2:7</reference>), reserved for the great work he contemplated.<div eID="gen5512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5513" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.6-1Chr.22.19">1Ch 22:6-19</reference>. He Instructs Solomon. <div eID="gen5513" type="x-p"/>
entries.4a8776709b694f568a9e0b4d83ec68523d088673: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3841"/><div sID="gen5514" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3841"/><hi type="bold">6. Then he called for Solomon ... and charged him--</hi>The earnestness and solemnity of this address creates an impression that it was given a little before the old king's decease. He unfolded his great and long cherished plan, enjoined the building of God's house as a sacred duty on him as his son and successor, and described the resources that were at command for carrying on the work. The vast amount of personal property he had accumulated in the precious metals [1Ch 22:14] must have been spoil taken from the people he had conquered, and the cities he had sacked. <chapter eID="1Chr.22"/>

entries.d49b1b010f6d9b26b209661e837e949824b0b6e5: <div eID="gen13731" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen13732" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen13733" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen13733" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen13732" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen13734" type="x-p"/> David makes great preparations for building a temple to the Lord, <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.1-1Chr.22.5">1Chr 22:1-5</reference>; gives the necessary directions to Solomon concerning it, <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.6-1Chr.22.16">1Chr 22:6-16</reference>; and exhorts the princes of Israel to assist in the undertaking, <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.17-1Chr.22.19">1Chr 22:17-19</reference>. <div eID="gen13734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13735" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen13735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13736" type="x-p"/> David said, This is the house of the Lord - Till a temple is built for his name, this place shall be considered the temple of God; and on this altar, and not on that at Gibeon, shall the burnt-offerings of Israel be made. David probably thought that this was the place on which God designed that his house should be built; and perhaps it was this that induced him to buy, not only the threshing-floor, but probably some adjacent ground also, as Calmet supposes, that there might be sufficient room for such a building.
entries.5b60e78612f233d16d8f91ecba1cd9145848be66: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen13736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13737" type="x-p"/> The strangers that were in the land - Those who had become proselytes to the Jewish religion, at least so far as to renounce idolatry, and keep what were called the seven Noahic precepts. These were to be employed in the more servile and difficult parts of the work: see on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.9.21">1Kgs 9:21</reference> (note). For the account of building the temple, see 1 Kings 5-9 (note), and the notes there.
entries.2b8c07ba9870471d8cfb6cc0f666edc55cd36aef: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen13737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13738" type="x-p"/> Irons - for the nails, etc. - Iron for bolts, bars, hinges, etc., etc.
entries.91e2984ffba8918495bb5d0d763cf6083f009efd: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen13738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13739" type="x-p"/> Solomon - is young and tender - He is as yet without complete knowledge and due experience; and it is necessary that I should make as much preparation for the work as I possibly can; especially as the house is to be exceedingly magnificent.
entries.66a7aa825265bdc6a3915bab5d7084eabc502f84: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen13739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13740" type="x-p"/> Thou hast shed blood abundantly - Heathens, Jews, and Christians, have all agreed that soldiers of any kind should have nothing to do with Divine offices. Shedding of human blood but ill comports with the benevolence of God or the spirit of the Gospel. <div eID="gen13740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13741" type="x-p"/> Aeneas, overpowered by his enemies, while fighting for his parents, his family, and his country, finding farther resistance hopeless, endeavors to carry off his aged father, his wife, young son, and his household gods; but as he was just come from slaughter, he would not even handle these objects of superstition, but confided them to his father, whom he took on his shoulders, and carried out of the burning of Troy. <div eID="gen13741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13742" type="x-p"/> Tu, genitor, cape sacra manu, patriosque penates: <div eID="gen13742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13743" type="x-p"/> Me bello tanto digressum, et caede recenti, <div eID="gen13743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13744" type="x-p"/> Attrectare nefas; donec me flumine vivo Abluero. <div eID="gen13744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13745" type="x-p"/> Aen. ii., ver. 717. "Our country gods, our relics, and the bands, <div eID="gen13745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13746" type="x-p"/> Hold you, my father, in your guiltless hands: <div eID="gen13746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13747" type="x-p"/> In me 'tis impious holy things to bear, <div eID="gen13747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13748" type="x-p"/> Red as I am with slaughter, new from war; <div eID="gen13748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13749" type="x-p"/> Till, in some living stream, I cleanse the guilt <div eID="gen13749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13750" type="x-p"/> Of dire debate, and blood in battle spilt." <div eID="gen13750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13751" type="x-p"/> Dryden. <div eID="gen13751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13752" type="x-p"/> See the note at the end of <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.25">2Sam 7:25</reference> (note).
entries.33196988acc14d824981e3c8a0ffb3fe9b3b8b80: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen13752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13753" type="x-p"/> His name shall be Solomon - שלמה Shelomoh, from שלם shalam, he was peaceable; and therefore, says the Lord, alluding to the name, I will give Peace, שלום Shalom, in his days.
entries.7ddb833d60e6f0c18aa1af9d71355f267c2a0325: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen13753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13754" type="x-p"/> In my trouble I have prepared - Notwithstanding ail the wars in which I have been engaged, all the treacheries with which I have been surrounded, all the domestic troubles with which I have been overwhelmed, I never lost sight of this great object, the building of a house for God, that his worship might be established in the land. I have curtailed my expenses, and have lived in comparative poverty that I might save all I possibly could for this building. <div eID="gen13754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13755" type="x-p"/> A hundred thousand talents of gold - A talent of gold weighed three thousand shekels, and was worth five thousand and seventy-five pounds, fifteen shillings, and seven pence half-penny. One hundred thousand such talents would therefore amount to five hundred and seven millions, five hundred and seventy-eight thousand, one hundred and twenty-five pounds sterling. These sums are variously computed by several writers. <div eID="gen13755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13756" type="x-p"/> A thousand thousand talents of silver - A talent of silver weighed three thousand shekels, and was worth three hundred and fifty-three pounds, eleven shillings, and ten pence. A thousand thousand, or a million, of such talents would amount to the immense sum of three hundred and fifty-three millions, five hundred and ninety-one thousand, six hundred and sixty-six pounds, thirteen shillings, and four pence, sterling; both sums amounting to eight hundred and sixty-one millions, one hundred and sixty-nine thousand, seven hundred and ninety-one pounds, thirteen shillings, and four pence. <div eID="gen13756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13757" type="x-p"/> Thou mayest add thereto - Save as I have saved, out of the revenues of the state, and thou mayest also add something for the erection and splendor of this house. This was a gentle though pointed hint, which was not lost on Solomon.
entries.206a264fee9fda5a289dd5ea6b03dc2fdfc47411: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen13757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13758" type="x-p"/> Is not the Lord your God with you? - "Is not the Word of the Lord your God your assistant?" - T. <div eID="gen13758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13759" type="x-p"/> Hath he not given you rest on every side? - David at this time was not only king of Judea, but had also subdued most of the surrounding nations. <div eID="gen13759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13760" type="x-p"/> Thus Solomon came to the Jewish throne with every possible advantage. Had he made a proper use of his state and of his talents, he would have been the greatest as well as the wisest of sovereigns. But alas! how soon did this pure gold become dim! He began with an unlawful matrimonial connection; this led him to a commerce that was positively forbidden by the law of God: he then multiplied his matrimonial connections with heathen women; they turned his heart away from God, and the once wise and holy Solomon died a fool and an idolater.  <chapter eID="1Chr.22"/> <div eID="gen13760" type="x-p"/>

entries.9bd87f41b96e93c295ea952b786cae9154dd50ab: <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.1">1Ch 22:1</reference> <div eID="gen5815" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5816" type="x-p"/> With this chapter commences the second section of the history of David’s kingship, viz., the account of the preparations, dispositions, and arrangements which he made in the last years of his reign for the establishment of his kingdom in the future under his successors. All these preparations and dispositions had reference to the firm establishment of the public worship of the Lord, in which Israel, as the people and congregation of Jahve, might show its faithfulness to the covenant, so as to become partakers of the divine protection, and the blessing which was promised. To build the temple-this desire the Lord had not indeed granted the fulfilment of to David, but He had given him the promise that his son should carry out that work. The grey-haired king accordingly made preparations, after the site of the house of God which should be built had been pointed out to him, such as would facilitate the execution of the work by his successor. Of these preparations our chapter treats, and in it we have an account how David provided the necessary labour and materials for the building of the temple (<reference osisRef="1Chr.22.2-1Chr.22.5">1Ch 22:2-5</reference>), committed the execution of the work in a solemn way to his son Solomon (<reference osisRef="1Chr.22.6-1Chr.22.16">1Ch 22:6-16</reference>), and called upon the chiefs of the people to give him their support in the work (<reference osisRef="1Chr.22.17-1Chr.22.19">1Ch 22:17-19</reference>).
entries.de1808e2589afe5d5a3bb2d9f1ee292281a1e4d5: <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.2">1Ch 22:2</reference> <hi type="italic">Workmen and materials for the building of the temple</hi>. - 1Ch 22:2. In order to procure the necessary workmen, David commanded that the strangers in the land of Israel should be gathered together, and, as we learn from <reference osisRef="2Chr.2.16">2Ch 2:16</reference>, also numbered. הגּרים, the strangers, are the descendants of the Canaanites whom the Israelites had not destroyed when they took possession of the land, but had reduced to bondage (<reference osisRef="2Chr.8.7-2Chr.8.9">2Ch 8:7-9</reference>; 1Ki 9:20-22). This number was so considerable, that Solomon was able to employ 150,000 of them as labourers and stone-cutters (1Ki 5:15.; 2Ch 2:16.). These strangers David appointed to be stone-cutters, to hew squared stones, גזית אבני (see on 1Ki 5:18).
entries.b12fd47cea7702d5d20ec8d93e42cde70c8f4bff: <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.3">1Ch 22:3</reference> <div eID="gen5816" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5817" type="x-p"/> Iron and brass he prepared in abundance: the iron for the nails of the doors, i.e., for the folding-doors of the gates, i.e., partly for the pivots (<hi type="italic">Zapfen</hi>) on which the folding-doors turned, partly to strengthen the boards of which doors were made; as also for the מחבּרות, literally, things to connect, i.e., properly iron cramps.
entries.468f001d67ae6478d45100029b408fe205d75a50: <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.4">1Ch 22:4</reference> <div eID="gen5817" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5818" type="x-p"/> The Tyrians sent him cedar trees or beams in abundance, probably in exchange for grain, wine, and fruit of various sorts, which the Phoenicians obtained from the Israelites; cf. Movers, <hi type="italic">Phönizier,</hi> iii. 1, S. 88ff. Sidonians and Tyrians are named to denote the Phoenicians generally, as in Ezr 3:7. When Solomon began to build the temple, he made a regular treaty with Hiram king of Tyre about the delivery of the necessary cedar wood, 1Ki 5:15.
entries.d6ac069dbbac5e13726f19d85e73f726b105033b: <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.5">1Ch 22:5</reference> <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.5">1Ch 22:5</reference> gives in substance the reason of what precedes, although it is connected with it only by ו consec. Because his son Solomon was still in tender youth, and the building to be executed was an exceedingly great work, David determined to make considerable preparation before his death. ורך נער ור, <hi type="italic">puer et tener</hi>, repeated in <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.1">1Ch 29:1</reference>, indicates a very early age. Solomon could not then be quite twenty years old, as he was born only after the Syro-Ammonite war (see on <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.24">2Sa 12:24</reference>), and calls himself at the commencement of his reign still קטן נער   (1Ki 3:7). The word נער may of itself denote not merely a boy, but also a grown youth; but here it is limited to the boyish age by the addition of ורך. Berth. wrongly compares <reference osisRef="Exod.33.11">Exo 33:11</reference>, where נער denotes not a boy, but a lad, i.e., a servant. In the succeeding clause ליהוה לבנות is to be taken relatively: and the house which is to be built to the Lord is to be made great exceedingly (למעלה, see on <reference osisRef="1Chr.14.2">1Ch 14:2</reference>), for a name and glory for all lands, i.e., that it might be to the Lord for whom it should be built for an honour and glory in all lands. לו נא אכינה, I will (= therefore will I) prepare for him (Solomon), <hi type="italic">scil.</hi> whatever I can prepare to forward this great work.
entries.9c706d9bb3891cbf26d954cbfc7457a2733b8473: <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.6-1Chr.22.10">1Ch 22:6-10</reference> <hi type="italic">Solomon commissioned to build the temple</hi>. - 1Ch 22:6. Before his death (<reference osisRef="1Chr.22.5">1Ch 22:5</reference>) David called his son Solomon, in order to commit to him the building of the temple, and to press it strongly upon him, <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.7">1Ch 22:7</reference>-10. With this design, he informs him that it had been his intention to build a temple to the Lord, but the Lord had not permitted him to carry out this resolve, but had committed it to his son. The <hi type="italic">Keri</hi> בּני (<reference osisRef="1Chr.22.7">1Ch 22:7</reference>) is, notwithstanding the general worthlessness of the corrections in the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi>, probably to be preferred here to the Keth. בּנו, for בּנו might have easily arisen by the copyist’s eye having wandered to בּנו לשׁלמה, 1Ch 22:6. David’s addressing him as בּני is very fitting, nay, even necessary, and not contrary to the following אני. לבבי עם, it was with my heart, i.e., I had intended, occurs indeed very often in the Chronicle, e.g., <reference osisRef="1Chr.28.2">1Ch 28:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.1.11">2Ch 1:11</reference>; 2Ch 6:7., <reference osisRef="1Chr.9.1">1Ch 9:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.24.4">1Ch 24:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.10">1Ch 29:10</reference>, but is also found in other books where the sense demands it, e.g., <reference osisRef="Josh.14.7">Jos 14:7</reference>; 1Ki 8:17., 1Ch 10:2. In עלי ויהי, There came to me the word of Jahve (<reference osisRef="1Chr.22.8">1Ch 22:8</reference>), it is implied that the divine word was given to him as a command. The reason which David gives why the Lord did not allow him to build the temple is not stated in 1 Chron 17 (2 Sam 7), to which David here refers; instead of the reason, only the promise is there communicated, that the Lord would first build him a house, and enduringly establish his throne. This promise does not exclude the reason stated here and in <reference osisRef="1Chr.28.3">1Ch 28:3</reference>, but rather implies it. As the temple was only to be built when God had enduringly established the throne of David, David could not execute this work, for he still had to conduct wars - wars, too, of the Lord - for the establishment of his kingdom, as Solomon also states it in his embassy to Hiram. Wars and bloodshed, however, are unavoidable and necessary in this earth for the establishment of the kingdom of God in opposition to its enemies, but are not consonant with its nature, as it was to receive a visible embodiment and expression in the temple. For the kingdom of God is in its essence a kingdom of peace; and battle, or war, or struggle, are only means for the restoration of peace, the reconciliation of mankind with God after the conquest of sin and all that is hostile to God in this world. See on 2Sa 7:11. David, therefore, the man of war, is not to build the temple, but (1Ch 22:9.) his son; and to him the Lord will give peace from all his enemies, so that he shall be מנוּחה אישׁ, a man of rest, and shall rightly bear the name Shelomo (Solomon), i.e., Friederich (rich in peace, Eng. Frederick), for God would give to Israel in his days, i.e., in his reign, peace and rest (שׁקט). The participle נולד after הנּה has the signification of the future, shall be born; cf. 1Ki 13:2. מנוּחה אישׁ, not a man who procures peace (<reference osisRef="Jer.51.59">Jer 51:59</reference>), but one who enjoys peace, as the following לו והניחותי shows. As to the name שׁלמה, see on 2Sa 12:24. Into <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.10">1Ch 22:10</reference> David compresses the promise contained in <reference osisRef="1Chr.17.12">1Ch 17:12</reference> and 1Ch 17:13.
entries.6f9b045250938af5fe4254aa3a39295d4f8780a3: <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.11-1Chr.22.12">1Ch 22:11-12</reference> <div eID="gen5818" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5819" type="x-p"/> After David had so committed to his son Solomon the building of the temple, as task reserved and destined for him by the divine counsel, he wishes him, in <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.11">1Ch 22:11</reference>, the help of the Lord to carry out the work. והצלחתּ, <hi type="italic">ut prospere agas et felici successu utaris</hi> (J. M. Mich.), cf. Jos 1:8. על דּבּר of a command from on high; cf. עלי .f, 1Ch 22:8. Above all, however, he wishes (<reference osisRef="1Chr.22.12">1Ch 22:12</reference>) him right understanding and insight from God (וּבינה שׂכל, so connected in <reference osisRef="2Chr.2.11">2Ch 2:11</reference> also), and that God may establish him over Israel, i.e., furnish him with might and wisdom to rule over the people Israel; cf. 2Sa 7:11. ולשׁמור, “to observe” = and mayest thou observe the law of Jahve; not thou must keep (Berth.), for ולשׁמור is to be regarded as a continuation of the <hi type="italic">verb. finit.</hi>; cf. Ew. §351, c, S. 840.
entries.a9cdf92cbda0d892e0fc4ba4378f2aad8e4d5445: <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.13">1Ch 22:13</reference> <div eID="gen5819" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5820" type="x-p"/> The condition of obtaining the result is the faithful observing of the commands of the Lord. The speech is filled with reminiscences of the law, cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.7.11">Deu 7:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.11.32">Deu 11:32</reference>; and for the exhortation to be strong and of good courage, cf. <reference osisRef="Deut.31.6">Deu 31:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.1.7">Jos 1:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Josh.1.9">Jos 1:9</reference>, etc.
entries.f160aabd666b09292cd6eca19a7019a159fd3c85: <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.14-1Chr.22.16">1Ch 22:14-16</reference> <div eID="gen5820" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5821" type="x-p"/> In conclusion (<reference osisRef="1Chr.22.14-1Chr.22.16">1Ch 22:14-16</reference>), David mentions what materials he has prepared for the building of the temple. בּעניי, not, in my poverty (lxx, Vulg., Luth.), but, by my painful labour (<hi type="italic">magna molestia et labore</hi>, Lavat.); cf. <reference osisRef="Gen.31.42">Gen 31:42</reference>, and the corresponding בּכל־כּוחי,   1Ch 29:2. Gold 100,000 talents, and silver 1,000,000 talents. As the talent was 3000 shekels, and the silver shekel coined by the Maccabees, according to the Mosaic weight, was worth about 2s. 6d., the talent of silver would be about £375, and 1,000,000 talents £375,000,000. If we suppose the relative value of the gold and silver to be as 10 to 1,100,000 talents of gold will be about the same amount, or even more, viz., about £450,000,000, i.e., if we take the gold shekel at thirty shillings, according to Thenius’ calculation. Such sums as eight hundred or eight hundred and twenty-five millions of pounds are incredible. The statements, indeed, are not founded upon exact calculation or weighing, but, as the round numbers show, only upon a general valuation of those masses of the precious metals, which we must not think of as bars of silver and gold, or as coined money; for they were in great part vessels of gold and silver, partly booty captured in war, partly tribute derived from the subject peoples. Making all these allowances, however, the sums mentioned are incredibly great, since we must suppose that even a valuation in round numbers will have more or less correspondence to the actual weight, and a subtraction of some thousands of talents from the sums mentioned would make no very considerable diminution. On the other hand, it is a much more important circumstance that the above estimate of the value in our money of these talents of silver rests upon a presumption, the correctness of which is open to well-founded doubts. For in that calculation the weight of the Mosaic or holy shekel is taken as the standard, and it is presumed that the talents weighed 3000 Mosaic shekels. But we find in <reference osisRef="2Sam.14.26">2Sa 14:26</reference> mention made in David’s time of another shekel, “according to the kings’ weight,” whence we may with certainty conclude that in common life another shekel than the Mosaic or holy shekel was in use. This shekel according to the king’s weight was in all probability only half as heavy as the shekel of the sanctuary, i.e., was equal in weight to a Mosaic beka or half-shekel. This is proved by a comparison of 1Ki 10:17 with <reference osisRef="2Chr.9.16">2Ch 9:16</reference>, for here three golden minae are reckoned equal to 300 shekels-a mina containing 100 shekels, while it contained only 50 holy or Mosaic shekels. With this view, too, the statements of the Rabbins agree, e.g., R. Mosis Maimonidis <hi type="italic">constitutiones de Siclis, quas</hi> - <hi type="italic">illustravit Joa. Esgers.</hi>, Lugd. Bat. 1718, p. 19, according to which the שלחול שקל or המדינה שׁקל, i.e., the common or civil shekel, is the half of the הקדשׁ שׁקל. That this is the true relation, is confirmed by the fact that, according to <reference osisRef="Exod.38.26">Exo 38:26</reference>, in the time of Moses there existed silver coins weighing ten gera (half a holy shekel) called beka, while the name beka is found only in the Pentateuch, and disappears at a later time, probably because it was mainly such silver coins of ten gera which were in circulation, and to them the name shekel, which denotes no definite weight, was transferred. Now, if the amounts stated in our verse are reckoned in such common shekels (as in <reference osisRef="2Chr.9.16">2Ch 9:16</reference>), the mass of gold and silver collected by David for the building of the temple would only be worth half the amount above calculated, i.e., about £375,000,000 or £400,000,000. But even this sum seems enormously large, for it is five times the annual expenditure of the greatest European states in our day.<note placement="foot">According to Otto Hübner, <hi type="italic">Statistical Table of all Lands of the Earth</hi>, 18th edition, Frankf. a M. 1869, the yearly expenditure of Great Britain and Ireland (exclusive of the extra-European possessions) amounts to a little over £70,000,000; of the French Empire, to £85,000,000; of Russia, to about £78,000,000; of Austria and Hungary, to £48,500,000.</note> <div eID="gen5821" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5822" type="x-p"/> Yet the calculation of the income or expenditure of modern states is no proper standard for judging of the correctness of probability of the statements here made, for we cannot estimate the accumulation of gold and silver in the states and chief cities of Asia in antiquity by the budgets of the modern European nations. In the capitals of the Asiatic kingdoms of antiquity, enormous quantities of the precious metals were accumulated. Not to mention the accounts of Ktesias, Diodor. Sic., and others, which sound so fabulous to us now, as to the immense booty in gold and silver vessels which was accumulated in Nineveh and Babylon (see the table in Movers, <hi type="italic">die Phönizier,</hi> ii. 3, S. 40ff.), according to Varro, in Pliny, <hi type="italic">Hist. Nat.</hi> xxxii. 15, Cyrus obtained by the conquest of Asia a booty of 34,000 pounds of gold, besides that which was wrought into vessels and ornaments, and 500,000 talents of silver; and in this statement, as Movers rightly remarks, it does not seem probable that there is any exaggeration. In Susa, Alexander plundered the royal treasury of 40,000, according to other accounts 50,000 talents, or, as it is more accurately stated, 40,000 talents of uncoined gold and silver, and 9000 talents in coined darics. These he caused to be brought to Ecbatana, where he accumulated in all 180,000 talents. In Persepolis he captured a booty of 120,000 talents, and in Pasargada 6000 talents (see Mov. <hi type="italic">loc cit.</hi> S. 43). Now David, it is true, had not conquered Asia, but only the tribes and kingdoms bordering on Canaan, including the kingdom of Syria, and made them tributary, and had consecrated all the gold and silver taken as booty from the conquered peoples, from the Syrians, Moabites, Ammonites, Philistines, Amalekites, and Hadadezer the king of Zobah (2Sa 8:11.), to Jahve. Now, in consequence of the ancient connection between Syria and the rich commercial countries of the neighbourhood, great treasures of silver and gold had very early flowed in thither. According to <reference osisRef="2Sam.8.7">2Sa 8:7</reference>, the servants (i.e., generals) of King Hadadezer had golden shields, which David captured; and the ambassadors of King Toi of Hamath brought him vessels of silver, gold, and copper, to purchase his friendship.<note placement="foot">Apropos of the riches of Syria even in later times, Movers reminds us, S. 45, of the rich temple treasures - of the statue of Jupiter in Antioch, which was of pure gold and fifteen yards high, and of the golden statues in the temple at Hierapolis - and adds: “Even Antiochus the Great had immense treasures in his possession. The private soldiers in his army had their half-boots studded with gold nails, and their cooking utensils were of silver.” See the proofs, <hi type="italic">loc cit</hi>.</note> <div eID="gen5822" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5823" type="x-p"/> The other peoples whom David overcame are not to be regarded as poor in the precious metals. For the Israelites under Moses had captured so large a booty in gold rings, bracelets, and other ornaments from the nomadic Midianites, that the commanders of the army alone were able to give 16,750 shekels (i.e., over 5 1/2 talents of gold, according to the Mosaic weight) to the sanctuary as a consecrating offering (Num 31:48.). <div eID="gen5823" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5824" type="x-p"/> We cannot therefore regard the sums mentioned in our verse either as incredible or very much exaggerated,<note placement="foot">As Berth. for example does, expressing himself as follows: “In our verse, 100,000 talents of gold, 1,000,000 talents of silver, - a sum with which the debts of the European nations might almost be paid! It is absolutely inadmissible to take these at their literal value, and to consider them as a repetition, though perhaps a somewhat exaggerated one, of actual historical statements. They can have been originally nothing else than the freest periphrasis for much, an extraordinary quantity, such as may even yet be heard from the mouths of those who have not reflected on the value and importance of numbers, and consequently launch out into thousands and hundreds of thousands, in an extremely unprejudiced way.” On this we remark: (1) The assertion that with the sums named in our verse the debts of the European nations could be paid, is an enormous exaggeration. According to O. Hübner’s tables, the national debt of Great Britain and Ireland alone amounts to £809,000,000, that of France to £564,000,000, that of Russia to £400,000,000, that of Austria to £354,000,000, and that of the kingdom of Italy to £258,000,000; David’s treasures, consequently, if the weight be taken in sacred shekels, would only have sufficed to pay the national debt of Great Britain and Ireland. (2) The hypothesis that the chronicler, without reflecting on the value and importance of numbers, has launched out into thousands and hundreds of thousands, presupposes such a measure of intellectual poverty as is irreconcilable with evidences of intellect and careful planning such as are everywhere else observable in his writing.</note> nor hold the round sums which correspond to the rhetorical character of the passage with certainty to be mistakes.<note placement="foot">As proof of the incorrectness of the above numbers, it cannot be adduced “that, according to 1Ki 10:14, Solomon’s yearly revenue amounted to 666 talents of gold, i.e., to about £3,000,000 in gold; that the queen of Sheba presented Solomon with 120 talents of gold, 1Ki 10:10; <reference osisRef="2Chr.9.9">2Ch 9:9</reference>; and King Hiram also gave him a similar amount, 1Ki 9:14; all of which sums the context shows are to be considered extraordinarily great” (Berth.). For the 666 talents of gold are not the entire annual income of Solomon, but, according to the distinct statement of the Biblical historian, are only the annual income in gold, exclusive of the receipts from the customs, and the tributes of the subject kings and tribes, which were probably more valuable. The 120 talents of the queen of Sheba are certainly a very large present, but Solomon would give in return not inconsiderable presents also. But the quantities of silver and gold which David had collected for the building of the temple had not been saved out of his yearly income, but had been in great part captured as booty in war, and laid up out of the tribute of the subject peoples. A question which would more readily occur than this is, Whether such enormous sums were actually necessary for the temple? But the materials necessary to enable us to arrive at even a proximate estimate of this building are entirely wanting. The building of a stone temple from 60 to 70 yards long, 20 yards broad, and 30 yards high, would certainly not have cost so much, notwithstanding that, as we read in 2Ch 3:8., 650 talents of gold were required to gild the inner walls of the Holy Place, and at the same rate 2000 talents must have been required to gild the inside of the Sanctuary, which was three times as large; and notwithstanding the great number of massive gold vessels, e.g., the ten golden candlesticks, for which alone, even if they were no larger and heavier than the candlesticks in the tabernacle, ten talents of gold must have been required. But there belonged to the temple many subordinate buildings, which are not further described; as also the colossal foundation structures and the walls enclosing the temple area, the building of which must have swallowed up millions, since Solomon sent 70,000 porters and 80,000 stone-hewers to Lebanon to procure the necessary materials. Consul Rosen has recently indeed attempted to show, in <hi type="italic">das Haram von Jerusalem und der Tempelplatz des Moria,</hi> Botha (1866), that there is reason to suppose that the temple area was enlarged to the size it is known to have had, and surrounded by a wall only by Herod; but he has been refuted by Himpel in the <hi type="italic">Tübinger theol. Quartalschr</hi>. 1867, S. 515f., who advances very weighty reasons against his hypothesis. Finally, we must have regard to the statement in 1Ki 7:51 and <reference osisRef="2Chr.5.1">2Ch 5:1</reference>, that Solomon, after the building was finished, deposited the consecrated silver and gold collected by his father David among the temple treasures. Whence we learn that the treasures collected by David were not intended merely for the building of the House of God.</note> <div eID="gen5824" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5825" type="x-p"/> Brass and iron were not weighed for abundance; cf. 1Ch 22:3. Beams of timber also, and stones - that is, stones hewed and squared - David had prepared; and to this store Solomon was to add. That he did so is narrated in 2 Chr. 2.
entries.543370eb0b3b1fd239c55759330ff3332eb361bc: <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.17-1Chr.22.19">1Ch 22:17-19</reference> <hi type="italic">Exhortation to the princes of Israel to assist in the building of the temple.</hi> - David supports his exhortation by calling to remembrance the proofs of his favour which the Lord had showed His people. The speech in <reference osisRef="1Chr.22.18">1Ch 22:18</reference> is introduced without לאמר, because it is clear from the preceding דויד ויצו that the words are spoken by David: “The Lord has given you peace round about; for He has given the inhabitants of the land into my hands, and the land is subdued before Jahve and before His people.” The subdued land is Canaan: the inhabitants of the land are, however, not the Israelites over whom the Lord had set David as king, for the words בּידי נתן cannot apply to them, cf. 1Ch 14:10., <reference osisRef="Josh.2.24">Jos 2:24</reference>; it is the Canaanites still left in the land in the time of David, and other enemies, who, like the Philistines, possessed parts of the land, and had been subdued by David. On הארץ נככּשׁה, cf. <reference osisRef="Josh.18.1">Jos 18:1</reference>; Num 32:22, Num 32:29. This safety which the Lord had granted them binds them in duty to seek Him with all their heart, and to build the sanctuary, that the ark and the sacred vessels may be brought into it. The ל in לבּית is not a sign of the accusative (Berth.), for הביא is not construed with <hi type="italic">accus. loci</hi>, but generally with אל, for which, however, so early as <reference osisRef="Josh.4.5">Jos 4:5</reference>, ל is used, or it is construed with the <hi type="italic">acc</hi>. and ה <hi type="italic">locale</hi> - הבּיתה, <reference osisRef="Gen.19.10">Gen 19:10</reference>; Gen 43:17. Enumeration and Arrangement of the Levites According to Their Divisions and Employments - 1 Chronicles 23-26 <div eID="gen5826" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5827" type="x-p"/> These four chapters give a connected view of the condition of the Levites towards the end, i.e., in the fortieth year, of David’s reign (cf. <reference osisRef="1Chr.23.1">1Ch 23:1</reference> and <reference osisRef="1Chr.26.31">1Ch 26:31</reference>), and of the sections into which they were divided according to their various services. This review begins with a statement of the total number belonging to the tribe of Levi according to the census then undertaken, and their divisions according to the duties devolving upon (<reference osisRef="1Chr.23.2-1Chr.23.5">1Ch 23:2-5</reference>); which is followed by an enumeration of the heads of the fathers'-houses into which the four families of Levites had branched out (23:6-23), together with a short review of their duties (<reference osisRef="1Chr.23.24-1Chr.23.32">1Ch 23:24-32</reference>). Thereafter we have: 1. In 1 Chron 24, a catalogue of the Aaronites, i.e., of the priests, who were divided into twenty-four classes, corresponding to the sons of Eleazar and Ithamar, and were appointed to perform the service in succession, according as it was determined by lot, special mention being made of the heads of these twenty-four classes; and a catalogue of the heads of the fathers'-houses of the other descendants of Levi, in an order of succession, which was likewise settled by lot (<reference osisRef="1Chr.24.20-1Chr.24.31">1Ch 24:20-31</reference>). Then, 2. In 1 Chron 25 we have a catalogue of the twenty-four orders of Levitic musicians, in an order fixed by lot. And, 3. In 1 Chron 26 the classes of doorkeepers (vv. 1-19), the administrators of the treasures of the sanctuary (<reference osisRef="1Chr.26.20-1Chr.26.28">1Ch 26:20-28</reference>), and the officials who performed the external services (<reference osisRef="1Chr.26.29-1Chr.26.32">1Ch 26:29-32</reference>).  <chapter eID="1Chr.22"/> <div eID="gen5827" type="x-p"/>
